chief_complaint: sudden widespread itchy hives lasting few hours each
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden widespread itchy hives lasting few hours each. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he came down with mild food poisoning or reacted to some spoiled seafood he ate over the weekend.
concerns: He is worried that the swelling might suddenly spread inward to his throat and cut off his breathing.
expectations: He hopes to receive a fast-acting allergy shot or pills to clear the welts quickly and a blood test to identify the trigger.

core_concepts: Acute urticaria is a mast-cell-mediated eruption of pruritic, transient wheals lasting under six weeks, most often triggered by a viral infection, food, medication, or insect sting.
Each individual wheal typically fades within 24 hours, but new lesions can continue to appear for the duration of the episode.
Most cases are self-limited and idiopathic; extensive allergy workup is not routinely needed unless a specific trigger is strongly suspected from the history.
The clinical priority is distinguishing isolated cutaneous urticaria from anaphylaxis, which requires airway, respiratory, or cardiovascular involvement plus emergency treatment.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden widespread itchy hives lasting few hours each

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden widespread itchy hives lasting few hours each. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Scattered blanching, erythematous wheals of varying size; no angioedema, stridor, or hemodynamic instability.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the accompanying fatigue signals a serious systemic illness rather than a nonspecific viral or inflammatory trigger.
Ordering extensive allergy testing during the acute episode instead of first identifying a likely trigger from the history.
Withholding antihistamines because the hives look mild, delaying relief and symptom control.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to anaphylaxis (if airway/circulatory symptoms present) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Throat tightness, wheeze, or dizziness accompanying the hives.
management_principles: Start a non-sedating oral second-generation antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine) at standard dose, up-titrating if needed.
Identify and remove or avoid any likely trigger (new food, medication, or recent infection).
Advise avoiding aggravating factors such as hot showers or tight clothing that can worsen itching.
Educate on red-flag symptoms (throat tightness, wheeze, dizziness) that would require emergency care.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Scattered blanching, erythematous wheals of varying size; no angioedema, stridor, or hemodynamic instability.

Advise avoiding hot showers or tight clothing that can worsen itching. 4. Educate on red-flag symptoms that would require emergency care.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical presentation and course of acute urticaria
Distinguish acute urticaria from anaphylaxis and chronic urticaria
Select appropriate first-line antihistamine therapy and trigger-avoidance counseling for acute urticaria

teaching.one_liner: A sudden outbreak of itchy hives lasting less than six weeks, usually from a transient trigger such as a food, infection, or medication.
red_flags: Throat tightness, wheeze, or dizziness accompanying the hives

must_ask.say: When did the hives start, and can you think of anything new — food, medicine, illness?
Does each welt fade within a few hours?
Any swelling of your lips or throat, or trouble breathing?
Have you tried anything, like antihistamines, and did it help?

history.answer: I suddenly broke out in itchy red bumps all over my body, and they keep appearing and disappearing.
It started yesterday evening out of nowhere with a few spots on my chest, and it has gradually spread to my arms, legs, and back.
They are scattered on my chest, back, arms, and thighs, but not on my face, palms, or soles.
They look like raised red welts or mosquito bites of different sizes, swollen and puffy, but there are no blisters or scabs.
Each individual welt lasts about three or four hours and then fades away completely, but new ones keep popping up in other places.
They itch terribly, especially at night, but they do not burn, prickle, or cause sharp pain.
Taking a warm shower made the itching a lot worse, while placing a cool wet towel on my skin gave a little relief.
I ate shrimp stir-fry for dinner about two hours before the rash began, which I rarely eat, but I have not used any new soaps, lotions, or detergents.
No, I have not started any new antibiotics, pain relievers, gout pills, or herbal supplements.
No, my breathing has been completely normal with no shortness of breath, wheezing, or chest tightness.
No, my lips, tongue, and throat feel completely normal, and I can swallow without any difficulty.
No, I have not felt dizzy, faint, or lightheaded at all.
I have not had any fever or chills, though I have been feeling unusually tired and worn out all over.
No, I do not have any sores, ulcers, or blisters in my mouth, eyes, or private areas.
No, my skin is not peeling off, and none of the spots look dark purple or like bruises.
No, my joints feel fine without any pain or swelling, and my nails look completely normal.
No, I haven't been hiking, traveled recently, or noticed any insect or bug bites.
No one at home or at my office has any rash or itching like this.
I have never had an outbreak like this before in my life.
No, I do not have asthma, eczema, or allergic rhinitis.
I haven't applied any steroid creams or taken any allergy pills yet because I wanted a doctor to look at it first.
I have been in a monogamous relationship with my partner for two years, and neither of us has had any sores, ulcers, or discharge.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially, maybe a beer or two once a month.
I work as an office clerk and live alone in an apartment.
No one in my family has a history of chronic hives, asthma, eczema, or severe allergies.

I thought maybe I ate some bad takeout or reacted to some seafood over the weekend that poisoned my system. I'm really scared that the next time these welts break out, my throat will swell shut and I won't be able to breathe.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and comfortable appearance without acute distress, tachypnea, or audible stridor.
No conjunctival injection, periorbital edema, or scleral icterus.
Oral mucosa and lips are normal without swelling of the lips, tongue, or uvula.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, stridor, or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Multiple erythematous, raised, edematous wheals of varying sizes scattered across the trunk and extremities that blanch completely with pressure; no purpura, blisters, or skin peeling.
